Tell me in about 200 words why people in India are switching to UPI, with a short list of 3 reasons
12:42 PM

UPI has become India's default way to pay because it is free, instant and works on almost any phone. Instead of carrying cash or cards, people scan a QR code or type a number, and the money moves from bank to bank in seconds. That has suited everyone, from big-city shoppers to the chai seller on the corner.

Three main reasons:

Costs nothing for most people. Sending and receiving money between individuals is free, and small shops don't pay card fees, so even a ₹10 sale is worth taking digitally.
Fast and simple. One scan, one PIN, and the payment is done at any hour, including holidays. There is no need to share bank details or wait for a transfer to clear.
Works everywhere. Any bank account can link to any UPI app, so a shopkeeper and a customer don't need to use the same one. Its reach now covers small towns, bills, rent, tickets and online shopping.

Trust has helped too. Because UPI is run on a common national system and backed by the banks, people feel confident using it, and habit has done the rest. Once friends, family and local shops all accept it, going back to cash feels slow and inconvenient.
